title: The High and Holy One Dwells with the Lowly
summary: The righteous die unnoticed while God's people give themselves to idolatry: sexual rites under sacred trees, child sacrifice in the valleys, offerings to smooth stones, and trips to Molech and the underworld. God exposes their works as worthless, but promises that whoever takes refuge in him will inherit the land. Then the high and holy God, who inhabits eternity, declares that he also dwells with the contrite and lowly, and promises healing and peace to those far and near, while the wicked remain like a restless sea.
story: Chapter 56 ended with blind watchmen and greedy shepherds. Chapter 57 shows the result of such leadership: the righteous perish unnoticed and the people turn to old idolatries. It is one of the harshest passages in the last part of Isaiah, and it shows that the problem that sent Israel into exile, idolatry and injustice, had not disappeared. Yet the chapter turns in verse 14 with the same call heard in 40:3, to prepare the way, and it contains one of the Bible's most beautiful descriptions of God's nearness to the humble. It ends with the same refrain that closed chapter 48, that there is no peace for the wicked, marking another turn in the book's structure.
historical:
The practices condemned in verses 3 to 13 are well attested in Israel's history before the exile. Second Kings 21 describes King Manasseh of Judah (reigning in the first half of the seventh century BC) rebuilding high places, making his son pass through the fire, and practicing sorcery, and Jeremiah condemns child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:31). Scholars disagree about when this chapter was addressed. Some see it as reflecting Manasseh's reign or the period before the exile, perhaps an older oracle placed here; others argue that such practices persisted among those who remained in the land or revived after the return, so that the chapter addresses the postexilic community. The text itself does not settle the question.

Molech (verse 9) is also debated. Most read it as the name of a god associated with child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10). The German scholar Otto Eissfeldt argued in 1935 that the underlying word originally named a type of sacrifice rather than a god, a view that has had supporters and critics since. Some also take the word here as the Hebrew for king, referring to a foreign ruler courted with gifts.
cultural:
Canaanite religion was practiced at open-air shrines on hilltops and under large, leafy trees, which were associated with fertility (Deuteronomy 12:2; Hosea 4:13). Worship there could include sexual rites meant to secure the fertility of land and womb, which explains the chapter's mingling of adultery and idolatry. The smooth stones of the valley (verse 6) may refer to stones set up or worshiped in stream beds, or to the rocks where offerings to the dead were made; the precise practice is uncertain. The memorial behind the door (verse 8) may be a household idol or cultic symbol placed where the words of God's law were supposed to be written (Deuteronomy 6:9).

Descent to Sheol (verse 9) is the realm of the dead, and consulting the dead through mediums was forbidden to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-11). The image is of a people reaching everywhere, even into the underworld, for help and security, and never turning to the God who made them.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 and 2 are a brief lament over the righteous who die unnoticed. Verses 3 to 13 are a prophetic lawsuit: God summons the idolaters (“come here”), exposes their deeds in vivid, often sexual imagery of unfaithfulness, and pronounces sentence, contrasting the wind that carries off their idols with the land promised to those who take refuge in him. Verses 14 to 21 are a word of salvation, built around the self-description of God in verse 15, which balances height and lowliness in carefully matched lines: high and lifted up, yet with the contrite; holy, yet reviving the lowly. The closing verses contrast peace for those near and far with the churning sea of the wicked, and the final line repeats 48:22.

outline.t: Children of the sorceress: idolatry under every tree
Idols carried off by the wind; refuge in the LORD
The high and holy One dwells with the contrite

doctrines.note: The chapter shows idolatry as unfaithfulness in the most personal terms, like adultery, and as exhausting: the people wear themselves out chasing help from every source except God. Idols fail when they are needed most; a breath carries them off (verse 13).

God is high, lifted up, whose name is Holy, and he dwells in a high and holy place. Yet his holiness does not keep him distant from the broken; it brings him to them. The same verse holds his transcendence and his nearness together.

God dwells “with the oppressed and humble in spirit” (verse 15), and though he struck the rebellious in anger, he says, “I will heal him” (verse 18). Contrition, not achievement, is the condition of his presence.

words.note: Dakka, crushed, contrite. It is related to the verb used of the Servant in 53:5 and 53:10, crushed for our iniquities. Here God dwells with the one who is crushed in spirit. Psalm 51:17 uses a related form: a broken and crushed heart God will not despise.

Shafal, low, humble. It appears twice in verse 15, first in the phrase “humble in spirit” and then of the lowly whose spirit God restores. The word stands in deliberate contrast with rum, high, used of God in the same verse. The high God comes down to the low.

Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being in every relationship. The chapter uses it at both ends: the righteous enter peace in death (verse 2), and God promises “Peace, peace to those far and near” (verse 19). The doubled word expresses completeness, and the final verse denies it to the wicked.

christ: Paul quotes verse 19 in Ephesians 2:17, saying that Christ came and preached peace to those who were far away (Gentiles) and to those who were near (Jews), having made both one through the cross. The picture of the high God who dwells with the lowly is embodied, in Christian confession, in the incarnation: the eternal Son who took on flesh and humbled himself (Philippians 2:6-8). Jesus's teaching that the poor in spirit and those who mourn are blessed (Matthew 5:3-4) moves in the same direction as verse 15, though the Gospels do not quote this verse. The link to Ephesians is explicit; the others are thematic.

hard.q: Why does the chapter use such graphic sexual language for idolatry?
hard.a: Verses 7 and 8 describe Israel's unfaithfulness with frank sexual imagery, and modern readers can find it jarring or offensive, especially as it is addressed to the people as a woman. Several things help explain it. First, the prophets consistently described the covenant as a marriage, so unfaithfulness to God was naturally described as adultery (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). Second, the worship condemned here likely involved actual sexual rites at fertility shrines, so the language is partly literal. Third, the shock is intended: the prophet wants his hearers to feel the betrayal as God feels it. Some interpreters have raised concerns about how such imagery portrays women, and those concerns deserve a hearing. Others stress that the metaphor names the whole people, men as much as women, and that its aim is to expose betrayal, not to demean. The chapter's turn in verse 15 shows that the goal of the exposure is healing.

questions: Verse 10 says the people wore themselves out but never admitted it was hopeless. What things do people keep chasing long after they have stopped helping?
What does it mean to you that the God who inhabits eternity chooses to dwell with the crushed and lowly?
The chapter begins with the righteous dying unnoticed. Whose faithfulness around you goes unnoticed, and how might you honor it?
